title: You Can Feel It Before You Can Prove It
author: Andrea Chiarelli
summary: Chiarelli opens with a scenario every leader will recognize: the dashboard is green, milestones are technically on track, but the meetings feel different. Updates get vaguer. Meetings get shorter. Risk discussions quietly disappear from the agenda. People stop volunteering information, language formalizes, humor drains out, side conversations migrate from inside meetings to the hallway afterward, and key decisions get deferred without reason. These are not project indicators. They are trust indicators, and when trust erodes, information flow changes first. His middle section names the leader failure that turns wobble into collapse. Under uncertainty, capable, previously curious leaders often flip from curiosity to command. They stop asking what the team is learning and start declaring what the team is doing. Open discussions become status reports. Listening becomes directing. Chiarelli argues this is the exact moment when questions matter most, and the leader's own stress reflex is working against the right move. He provides language-level cues to catch the shift: ‘What are we missing?’ becoming ‘Here’s what we need to do,’ ‘Help me understand the delay’ becoming ‘Get this back on track by Friday,’ and ‘What’s your biggest concern?’ disappearing altogether. The cure is asking early, with genuine curiosity, before the crisis has hardened into blame. The back half is practitioner material. He offers a short bank of early questions that surface reality without assigning fault (‘What feels riskier than it looks on paper?’ ‘What’s one assumption we’re making that could be wrong?’ ‘What are we not talking about that we should be?’), and five habit mechanisms to make the asking consistent: reserve the last ten minutes of every status meeting for one of these questions, send hard questions in writing a day ahead, separate question time from decision time, ask the same person twice to get past the surface answer, and track the pattern of who speaks and where silence lands. When avoidance has already set in, he offers a Name-Normalise-Nudge repair protocol and a critical instruction: after asking, hold the silence. The first person to speak often unlocks the room. When they do, reward their candor visibly, because it teaches the team that honesty leads somewhere.
points: The central argument of this piece is grounded in the author's engagement with how real people think and act, not in idealized or abstract reasoning.
The takeaway is actionable,it can be implemented at the classroom or school level without waiting for policy change or external resources.
The piece challenges a common default assumption in education practice and offers a concrete alternative framed by evidence or lived experience.
The stakes are clear: what happens if leaders or teachers adopt this approach, and what is the cost of continuing the current default.
quotes: Projects don’t collapse overnight. They deteriorate through small misalignments and questions nobody wants to ask.
These are trust indicators: when trust erodes, information flow changes first. And this is when leaders matter most. Yes, this is also exactly when many of them stop asking questions.

Leaders worry that asking questions makes them look uninformed or indecisive. They fear losing control at the exact moment they need to maintain it. So they flip from curiosity to command: asking questions feels uncertain, whereas giving answers feels powerful.
The more uncertain things get, the more leaders need to ask questions. Yet the less likely they are to actually do it.

In our experience, there are two types of leaders when projects start going sideways. The first waits for certainty; the second looks for truth. The first manages the dashboard; the second manages the conversation.
Early questions sound different than crisis questions: in that they are not accusatory and take a genuine interest in understanding what is true. There’s no pointing fingers.

Silence after a question is information. It tells that people might be: Thinking (productive silence), Deciding if it’s safe to speak (cautious silence), Doubting your intentions and whether you really want to know (cynical silence). Your job is to hold the space and not fill it.

The best leaders offer clarity instead about what matters right now rather than about what is going to happen. And this creates confidence: not the fake confidence that comes from pretending everything’s under control, but the real confidence that comes from knowing your leader sees reality and won’t hide from it.” Archived from Andrea Chiarelli on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
